newsitem.title: USA: New storm moves into flood-stricken U.S. Northwest.
newsitem.headline: New storm moves into flood-stricken U.S. Northwest.

text.p: A new storm, forecast to pack winds of up to 70 mph (110 kph), moved over the U.S. Northwest on Tuesday, threatening more problems for a region hit by floods and mudslides after days of heavy rain and snow.
Rain and melting snow from the last storm swelled many rivers in western Washington state and Oregon to flood stage, inundating homes and streets in some areas.

About 445 evacuees spent the night in 16 shelters throughout Washington state, Gov. Mike Lowry's office said, and more than 40,000 Washington residents remained without electricity, according to Puget Sound Power and Light Co..
A series of storms that began last week is blamed for the deaths of 10 people in Washington and Oregon, mostly victims of car crashes and falling trees.

Homes were flooded in Centralia, about 70 miles (110 km) south of Seattle, where a river burst its banks. Roofs of dozens of buildings in western Washington collapsed under the weight of snow and a mudslide in Mukilteo, near Seattle, swept seven homes off their foundations.
Mudslides and avalanches blocked many highways throughout the western United States and several northern California rivers were expected to rise above flood stage.

Lowry has declared a state of emergency in 15 storm-hit counties in western Washington and state Insurance Commissioner Deborah Senn said an insurance industry group estimated insured storm damage to businesses and homes in Washington, Oregon and California at up to $250 million.
Rain was falling across the Pacific Northwest on Tuesday, but the full force of the storm was expected to hit later.

"We're expecting rain to develop (over Washington state) this afternoon becoming heavy at times this evening and New Year's Day," said Sten Tjaden, a forecaster with the National Weather Service in Seattle.

While forecasters were not expecting "too much of a deluge" from the approaching Pacific storm, flood warnings remained in effect for four rivers in western Washington and the new storm could push river levels higher, he said.
The storm was expected to bring winds of 40 to 50 miles (65 to 80 km) per hour with possible gusts up to 70 mph (110 kph), he said.
A high wind watch was issued for the Washington state coast and the northwestern part of the state. A winter weather advisory was in effect for the Cascade mountains.
Barbara Dunn, a spokeswoman for Washington Emergency Management, said the forecast high winds could cause new power outages and warm winds would melt snow more quickly, aggravating flooding.

The new storm also brought fears of flooding in Oregon, where the National Weather Service issued flood warnings for between 10 and 15 rivers, mostly in the west of the state. "It looks like the worst of the flooding will happen tomorrow and Thursday," Steve Todd, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Portland, said.
Many residents of Clackamas County, just south of Portland, Oregon, were sandbagging doorways to protect their homes from the rising waters of several rivers.
"There are some people that have water close enough to their homes that they've chosen to leave in various areas," said Casey Marley, emergency manager for Clackamas County.
"A lot of people have U-Hauls (moving vans) in their driveways to be ready to move out if the water continues to rise," she said.

The severe weather forced the closure of many roads throughout the region. Interstate 5, California's main north-south artery, was closed between Redding and Dunsmuir in northern California because of mudslides and Highway 1 on the central California coast was also closed by a mudslide.
All routes across the mountains between western and eastern Washington state remained closed due to avalanche danger.
In northern California, the National Weather Service extended flood warnings for the Russian and Napa rivers, swelled by days of heavy rain, through Thursday.
